findings.where: Hero, all of it (desktop-01, phone-01): the large mark, the name 'MARK · M · MOSELEY' in red Roman capitals with interpuncts, centred on flat grey stone
findings.fault: A dead person's name, cut in red capitals and centred on grey stone under an arch with a dovetailed tablet below, reads as a headstone or memorial plaque, not as a living advisor inviting contact. Nothing on the first screen is warm or personal: there is no face and no first-person line. All the warmth rests on one subline.
findings.who_objects: Mark, whose site is meant to show 'a personal, experienced advisor… approachable' (§5), not his epitaph. A development-bank visitor's first impression is also formal and sombre, not approachable.

findings.where: The mark in the hero and the nav lockup (desktop-01, phone-01); the palette's 'CUT · the aqueduct' swatch
findings.fault: The logo is recoloured. The arches are drawn in the palette's near-black #2A2925, not the logo grey #404040. The 'MMM INFRA' wordmark is set dark, not in logo blue #0070C0. The lockup also drops 'Moseley Infrastructure Advisory Services'. Logo blue does not appear in the palette, even as a logo-only colour.
findings.who_objects: Mark, whose logo 'stays' (client value 7, §4). The house rule says never recolour a logo: change its version or its ground, and only with the client's yes. Fixed logo colours must join the palette or be declared logo-only.

findings.where: Hero: the name heading and the 'WRITE TO MARK' button; also every heading on the page (the article title, 'CINZEL', 'LAID · WEIGHTY · SETTLED')
findings.fault: Minium, the one action colour, also colours every display heading. On the first screen the two-line red name, at about 60 px, outweighs the red button when you squint, so the action does not hold the view's strongest colour. Red stops meaning 'act here'. That contradicts the direction's own 'one accent only, and it flows to the action'.
findings.who_objects: A visitor deciding whether to get in touch: the one action competes with the heading's colour and size. The layout round would inherit a red that means two things.

findings.where: Article specimen, the pull quote (desktop-02/03, phone-02), against the hero button 'WRITE TO MARK'
findings.fault: One shape, the tabula ansata with its dovetail handles, carries two functions: the primary button and a static quote. The quote's version is an edged box with solid dark wedges, which reads as an outlined, secondary rung of the same button. Those wedges are also the heaviest marks in the article column, so the quote outweighs the title and body around it.
findings.who_objects: A reader of an article page who meets the framed, handled box and takes it for something to press. The house rule also objects: a button shape with a fill or edge is reserved for actions, and each look should mean one function.

findings.fault: A button that replays the animation is dressed as a link: tracked capitals with an underline, the carrier reserved for navigation. A visitor expects it to take them somewhere.
findings.who_objects: A visitor, who cannot tell from the look whether it replays in place or leaves the page. The layout round would inherit an underlined control that means two things.

findings.where: Article specimen title 'THE WORLD'S BEST PUBLIC-PRIVATE PARTNERSHIP LAW' (desktop-02, phone-02); also the dateline 'MMM INFRA BLOG NO. 8 · 18 SEPTEMBER 2024', the swatch names and the timeline table's column heads
findings.fault: Article titles are forced into all-caps tracked Cinzel. Even this six-word title runs three heavy red lines on desktop. A longer title an editor types would become a block of capitals that is slow to read. The tile also says Cinzel is for 'headings, the nav and the button only', yet uses it for small meta lines and table heads, where tracked capitals at that size read cramped.
findings.who_objects: Angélique, who adds posts with Mark's own long titles (client value 9), and readers in Read mode. The layout round also gets a rule the tile itself breaks.

findings.where: The tile as a whole: no photograph treatment anywhere (only a drawn stand-in texture)
findings.fault: The tile never shows how a photograph of Mark, or an editor's photo or video, sits on the granite ground, alongside the hard-edged, no-blending palette. The look's ability to show 'the man himself' (value 3), to take video (value 8) and to survive a lay editor's picture (value 9) is unanswered.
findings.who_objects: Mark, who wants to be seen and wants refreshed images from LinkedIn. Angélique, who will drop photos onto a mid-grey ground with no rule for framing or edges.
